title: Mobilisation without realignment
content:
Israel’s October 2026 elections produced a striking paradox. After three years of devastating wars, the failures surrounding 7 October, growing international isolation and deep domestic divisions, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc has lost its parliamentary majority. Yet Likud remains the largest party, and Netanyahu’s electoral performance was considerably stronger than many had anticipated.

According to the final count published by the Central Elections Committee on 29 October, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the Jewish-led opposition and a historic 19 for Arab parties; official certification is due on 4 November. This leaves 67 seats outside Netanyahu’s bloc, opening several possibilities for political change. However, the result should not be interpreted as an ideological shift towards the left. Much of the opposition consists of security-oriented centrists, nationalists and right-leaning liberals who explicitly distance themselves from Social Democracy.

title: If you want peace, prepare for equality
content: I have always been struck by how little attention we pay to patriarchal culture when we think about geopolitics. We analyse military budgets, alliances and power structures, yet we rarely ask what our very idea of power is, in a world built on masculine codes.

title: The Women, Peace and Security agenda amid shifting geopolitics
content: While the current conflictual and geopolitical environment makes the Women, Peace and Security agenda ever more relevant, it is being weakened by three mutually reinforcing processes: rising authoritarianism, the geopolitical instrumentalisation of (anti)gender, and the de-prioritisation of WPS by some of its traditional supporters.

title: The EU’s next WPS plan must act on tech, not just mention it
content:
The EU is drafting its next action plan on Women, Peace and Security, and technology will inevitably be part of it. The review of 122 national and regional action plans conducted by the Gender in Geopolitics Institute shows how that usually goes: technology is named as a threat, answered with awareness campaigns and never regulated. The EU can do better.

Technology has entered Women, Peace and Security (WPS) national action plans (NAP) fast: before 2018, none treated it as a security issue, but since 2025, 77 per cent do. Yet naming is not acting. Cybersecurity appears in 24 plans, but only 13 take concrete measures. Hybrid threats are mentioned in the plans of Croatia, Finland, Romania, Serbia and NATO, but no country acts on them. Not one technology measure has a target, a baseline or a budget. WPS plans have discovered technology, but they treat it as a danger to women that awareness campaigns can manage. They do not treat it as a power to be governed.

title: Not too small to matter
content:
Big states cannot cover it all. Smaller European states are stepping in, creating influence through niche politics. Ultimately, the argument that smaller states need to identify WPS areas where they can bring real added value has the potential to create influence based on outside-the-box thinking.

The Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda is often discussed through the lens of major European powers, such as the United Kingdom, France and Germany. And although smaller European states, especially the Nordic countries, are recognised as crucial WPS actors, the contributions of other countries, such as Austria, Ireland and Czechia, remain comparatively under the radar. Sustaining the WPS agenda requires stronger alliances and broader coalitions. It is therefore worth examining what smaller states can contribute when using their niche. The relevance lies not simply in filling gaps left by larger powers, but in how smaller states can use their specific expertise to foster impactful WPS practices.

title: Strong abroad, weak at home
content: Italy is one of the most committed middle-power implementers of the Women, Peace and Security agenda. Yet two decades of sustained engagement have had only limited effect in the domestic political arena and in the country’s foreign policy, even under its first female prime minister.

title: Serbia’s students defeat the machine
content:
The student list has won an outright majority in Serbia‘s snap parliamentary elections of 25 October 2026, ending fourteen years of rule by Aleksandar Vučić‘s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The result is less a routine alternation in power than a verdict on a model of governance – and it leaves Serbia‘s divided Social Democrats with uncomfortable questions.

According to the preliminary results of the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), the student list (‘Students Are Winning’) received 52.7 per cent of the vote and around 140 of the 250 seats in the National Assembly. The SNS-led coalition ‘Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia’ secured 39.2 per cent and around 104 seats. Apart from lists representing national minorities, which are exempt from the 3-per-cent-threshold, no other list entered parliament, producing the most concentrated assembly since the return of multiparty politics in 1990.

title: No peace in Lebanon without strong allies
content:
It came as little surprise that Lebanon once again became a battleground in the regional war between Israel and Iran. Even without Hezbollah’s half-hearted rocket fire, Israel would have invaded the South again. No one knows the business of preventive war better than Tel Aviv. While Iran, under attack, has fared far better in the Gulf than initially expected, Israel has largely succeeded in imposing its agenda in Lebanon. Yet this is unlikely to bring Lebanon any peace. Instead, the country risks jumping out of the frying pan and into the fire: Iranian hegemony is simply being replaced by Israeli hegemony.

Lebanon’s reformist government, of course, frames things differently. Sovereignty is its watchword. The fact that Lebanon is negotiating directly with the Israeli state under US auspices is presented as an expression of that sovereignty. This, however, is an excessively optimistic assumption – one that misreads both Israel’s new security doctrine and the region’s emerging alignments. These separate negotiations will not bring stability. Instead, they will ensure that Lebanon remains divided, weak and occupied.

title: Lessons from Maricarmen
content:
The case of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman from Madrid who passed away just days after being evicted from the apartment where she had lived – and for which she had paid – for decades, has resonated far beyond Spain’s borders. It has become a powerful symbol of a deeper crisis affecting our societies. For too long, housing has been treated primarily as a commodity rather than as a fundamental human right. For too long, we have been told that markets would regulate themselves and that public intervention would do more harm than good. Today, the evidence is undeniable: that approach has failed.

The question we must now confront is straightforward: what must we do to ensure that housing is guaranteed as a right, and not merely traded as an asset?

title: Housing: the basis of dignity and opportunities for all
content:
Housing is no longer just a local or national policy issue. Across Europe, housing costs increasingly shape people’s opportunities and influence the development of local economies. When people cannot afford to live where jobs are available, or young families struggle to find a home, the consequences extend well beyond the housing market. 

The scale of the problem is clear. Between 2010 and 2025, house prices in the EU increased by more than 60 per cent, while rents rose by almost 30 per cent. But the problem is not simply that housing has become more expensive. Across much of Europe, there is a structural shortage of affordable housing, alongside limited availability of social housing. 

The effects are visible across the economy. Workers find it harder to move to areas where their skills are needed. Young people are postponing leaving home, and families face growing difficulties staying in the communities where they have established their lives. What was once regarded mainly as a problem for low-income households increasingly affects the middle class.

title: Housing policies and territorial governance
content:
Housing policies and their effects are deeply connected to territorial governance. Talking about housing today means addressing not only home availability, but also competitiveness, public services, social cohesion, urban quality and balanced territorial development.

Housing directly contributes to a territory’s competitiveness. The availability of affordable, quality homes affects an area’s ability to attract and retain students, researchers, skilled workers and new talent. Universities, businesses and local economies can develop fully only if people can find housing at sustainable costs.

title: Europe gave us the freedom to move – without the right to stay
content:
Housing goes beyond building houses. It shapes where and how we live, work, raise our children, grow old – and which territories thrive or will be abandoned. It is about people. It is about dignity and trust. Housing is about hope: the promise that wherever you live, whoever you are, you are welcome in Europe and have a right to stay. 

Decades. Billions. This is what it took to build one of the EU’s greatest achievements: the freedom to move. But what freedom is this, when staying is no longer possible? What freedom when forced to move? A right to stay starts with a place to stay. One you call home. Someplace you can own, rent or simply afford. A place to build a life. That is why it is more than simply building houses. Housing is about life.
